agent-leak-inspector.documentation:
Input

Prompt audit: one system prompt or agent description, up to 1 MB. Leak check: a reference prompt (1 MB) and a response or transcript (5 MB). Plain text in any language; rules cover English, German and Russian.

Output

Each finding has a rule id, a group, a severity, the line, a short excerpt, an explanation and a suggested change. Recognized secrets and long values without spaces are masked in results and in the JSON report on a best-effort basis; the report never contains the full prompt or response.

Severity

High is reserved for explicit risks such as credentials, unlock passphrases, irreversible actions without confirmation, encoded copies of the prompt or secrets from the prompt in a response. A finding is a reason to look closer; no finding does not mean the prompt cannot be extracted.

Limits

The leak check compares words and word sequences, not meaning: a response that retells the prompt in other words, for example the same steps described with synonyms, is usually not found even when the content leaked. Translations, summaries and leaks spread over many answers can also be missed. Decoding covers Base64, hex and URL encoding up to two layers. The audit rules read the first 200,000 characters; the leak check compares up to 150,000 prompt words with up to 600,000 response words within about 15 seconds. Results say when a limit was reached. The prompt audit is lexical: it reads wording, not meaning. Prohibitions and negations in the same clause as the action (“never send chats to third parties”, “there are no secret discounts”) are not reported, but protective rules phrased unusually can still be reported by mistake, and risky rules phrased indirectly can be missed. Discounts and prices are reported only when the prompt shows that they are kept from customers.
agent-leak-inspector.faq:
Is my prompt sent to an AI model or to CyberDat?

No. This tool does not transmit the text you enter. Analysis is plain text comparison in your browser, the page blocks network connections from its scripts, and nothing is stored.

Does no finding mean my prompt cannot leak?

No. The tool only checks known patterns in the text you provide. Assume anything in a system prompt can be extracted and keep secrets and enforcement outside the prompt.

Does the leak check find a prompt retold in other words?

Usually not. The leak check compares words and word sequences, not meaning. A response that describes the same rules or steps with different words, a translation or a summary can be missed even when the content leaked; the overlap measure only gives a hint. Read the response yourself and assume that anything in a system prompt can be extracted.

Does a protective rule such as “never send chats to third parties” produce a finding?

Usually not. The audit recognizes a prohibition or negation in the same clause as the action, in English, German and Russian, and does not report it. The analysis is lexical, so a protective rule that is phrased unusually or spread over several sentences can still be reported; read each finding before acting on it.

Are all secret values hidden in the results?

No. Masking is best effort: recognized secrets and long values without spaces are shortened, but secrets in an unusual form can remain in excerpts. Review exports before sharing.

Does the tool generate prompts that extract system prompts?

No. It only analyzes text you paste and includes no attack prompts.

mitre-atlas-mapper.documentation:
Input

System profile: eight properties. Finding mapper: plain text up to 100,000 characters. Values that look like secrets are masked and are not used for matching.

Output

Candidate techniques grouped by ATLAS tactic, each with its parent technique, ATLAS maturity, description and the mitigations that ATLAS links to it. Add techniques to a selection, write notes and download it as Markdown or JSON with the ATLAS data version. The pasted text is never exported.

Data

MITRE ATLAS release 2026.10 (2026-10-28), Copyright MITRE, Apache License 2.0, converted from the official YAML by CyberDat. Case studies, entities and software are not included.

Limits

Mapping is done by rules and keywords; it misses what is described in other words or in another language and can propose a technique because a word appears in an unrelated sense. Simple denials close to a word (“there was no prompt injection”, “the bot refused to reveal its prompt”) and ordinary permitted use of a tool, a reference to a secret store or routine clean-up do not lead to an attack technique; protective or unusual wording can still produce a candidate. A general description of a poisoned tool or context gets the parent technique. No AI model is used.
mitre-atlas-mapper.faq:
Is my text sent to CyberDat, MITRE or an AI model?

No. This tool does not transmit the text you enter. The ATLAS data is part of the page and matching runs in your browser.

Does no match mean my system is safe?

No. No matching techniques found does not mean the system is not exposed. The mapping only recognizes known wording.

Why does a sentence like “there was no attack” give no technique?

A word that its own clause denies is not used as evidence, and ordinary permitted use of a tool is not treated as an attack. Only simple negations close to the word are recognized, so a denial phrased in an unusual way can still produce a candidate; check every candidate.

Is this an official MITRE tool?

No. The data comes from MITRE ATLAS under the Apache License 2.0; the mapping rules are CyberDat’s and are not endorsed by MITRE.
